title: Death may come first
hook: a half-written apology in your drafts; Shantideva says don't count on later
tomorrow: you leave it all behind. so why fight over any of it?

segments.voice: Yesterday: refuge in fear. Afraid, Shantideva named the fear and ran toward a protector. And the week behind it: a life that's hard to find, a good thought like lightning in the night, an elixir that turns base metal to gold, wish, then go, and offer the unowned.
screen: `A PROTECTOR.` → `HARD TO FIND · LIGHTNING · GOLD.` → `WISH, THEN GO · OFFER THE UNOWNED.`

segments.voice: There's a message sitting in a lot of drafts folders. It starts with I'm sorry, and stops halfway through the second line. The plan is to finish it when the moment is right: when things calm down, when they bring it up first, when the words come out better. The moment keeps not arriving. So yesterday's question: why not fix it later? Shantideva's reason fits in one blunt line.
screen: `I'M SORRY, AND THEN NOTHING.` → `WHEN THE MOMENT IS RIGHT.` → `WHY NOT LATER?`

segments.voice: Still inside his confession, after taking refuge, he says it plainly: death may come before my wrongs are mended. Death doesn't wait to see whether the job is done. Sick or healthy, he says, this life can't be trusted to last. It sounds grim, and he means it seriously. But read where it sits. It isn't there to frighten anyone into a corner. It's the reason under everything this week. Hard to find: so use it. Lightning: so look while it flashes. Wish, then go: so don't stop at the map. And now the plainest version: whatever needs mending, the mending has a clock on it, and nobody can see the clock. Shantideva's answer isn't panic. It's a short list of things worth doing today instead of someday. The apology. The call. The thing you owe someone, said straight. Mend it now.
screen: `DEATH MAY COME BEFORE IT'S MENDED.` · `IT DOESN'T WAIT FOR THE JOB.` · `THE REASON UNDER THE WHOLE WEEK.` · `NOT PANIC: A SHORT LIST.` · then, large: `MEND IT NOW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that needs mending: a word, a debt, a silence. Name what's been in the way. Then decide exactly when you'll do it, today, down to the hour, and see yourself doing it. Rest in that plan for the rest of the sit.
Death may come first: Shantideva's reason not to wait. It may arrive before a wrong is mended, so the mending belongs to today.
For the road: mend it now, while the door is still open. A week of the poem, done.

screen: `DAY 1463 COUNTS.` → `SHANTIDEVA'S GUIDE · 8 OF 50.` → `TOMORROW: YOU LEAVE IT ALL BEHIND. SO WHY FIGHT OVER ANY OF IT?`

howItsDone: Reflection on death is part of practice across Buddhist schools; many teachers pair it with the precious human life, as a reason to act well now rather than as a cause for fear.

original.note: Sanskrit: death. In chapter two Shantideva warns that it may come before his wrongs are mended.
